title: Subject pronouns before the verb
rule: Use subject pronouns such as I, you, he, she, it, we, and they before the verb.
explanation: Subject pronouns replace nouns and show who does the action.
error_reason: Her is an object pronoun, not a subject pronoun.
keywords: subject pronouns, i you he she it we they, pronouns

title: Present form of be
rule: Use am with I, is with he, she, and it, and are with you, we, and they.
explanation: The verb be changes with the subject.
error_reason: She takes is, not are.
keywords: verb be, am is are, be

title: Negative form of be
rule: Form negatives with am not, is not, or are not.
explanation: Add not after the correct form of be.
error_reason: The negative comes after am: am not.
keywords: am not, is not, are not, negative be

title: Questions with be
rule: In questions, put am, is, or are before the subject.
explanation: Invert the subject and the verb be.
error_reason: Questions with be need inversion.
keywords: questions with be, are you, is he, am i

title: Using a, an, and the
rule: Use a before consonant sounds, an before vowel sounds, and the for specific things.
explanation: Choose the article by sound and meaning.
error_reason: Book begins with a consonant sound, so use a.
keywords: a an the, articles

title: Regular plural nouns
rule: Add -s to make most plural nouns.
explanation: Use the plural form for more than one person or thing.
error_reason: Plural nouns usually need -s.
keywords: plurals, regular plurals, add s

title: Plural spelling changes
rule: Some nouns add -es, change y to ies, or have irregular plural forms.
explanation: Not all plurals are made the same way.
error_reason: Words ending in -x usually take -es.
keywords: plurals, boxes, babies, irregular plurals

title: Present simple for habits
rule: Use the present simple for routines, facts, and habits.
explanation: It describes things that happen regularly or are generally true.
correct_example_1: We go to work by bus.
correct_example_2: The sun rises in the east.
incorrect_example: We are go to work by bus.
corrected_example: We go to work by bus.
error_reason: The present simple does not use are with a main verb like go.
keywords: present simple, habits, routines, facts

title: Third person singular present simple
rule: Add -s or -es to the verb with he, she, or it in the present simple.
explanation: The verb changes for third person singular.
error_reason: He takes the third person singular verb form.
keywords: third person singular, present simple, s es

title: Do and does in negatives
rule: Use do not or does not with the base verb in present simple negatives.
explanation: Do not change the main verb after do or does.
error_reason: After does not, use the base verb play.
keywords: do not, does not, negatives, present simple

title: Questions with do and does
rule: Use do or does before the subject in present simple questions.
explanation: Do and does help make questions in the present simple.
error_reason: Present simple questions usually need do or does.
keywords: do does questions, present simple

title: Adjectives before nouns
rule: Put adjectives before nouns in English.
explanation: The adjective describes the noun.
error_reason: Adjectives usually come before the noun.
keywords: adjectives, order, before nouns

title: There is and there are
rule: Use there is for one thing and there are for more than one.
explanation: Choose the form by number.
correct_example_1: There is a table in the room.
error_reason: Two chairs is plural, so use there are.
keywords: there is, there are, singular plural

title: This, that, these, and those
rule: Use this and these for near things, and that and those for farther things.
explanation: Singular words are this and that; plural words are these and those.
error_reason: This is singular, but shoes is plural.
keywords: this that these those, demonstratives

title: Possessive adjectives
rule: Use my, your, his, her, its, our, and their before nouns.
explanation: Possessive adjectives show who owns something.
error_reason: Use possessive adjectives before nouns.
keywords: possessive adjectives, my your his her its our their

title: Countable and uncountable nouns
rule: Countable nouns can be singular or plural. Uncountable nouns are not usually plural.
explanation: Do not add a plural -s to most uncountable nouns.
error_reason: Rice is uncountable, so it is not usually plural.
keywords: countable uncountable nouns, singular plural, rice

title: Some and any
rule: Use some in positive sentences and any in questions and negatives.
explanation: Some is common in offers and requests too.
incorrect_example: I do not have some milk.
corrected_example: I do not have any milk.
error_reason: Any is normally used in negatives.
keywords: some any, questions negatives

title: A and an with singular countable nouns
rule: Use a or an with singular countable nouns when the noun is not specific.
explanation: Do not use a/an with plural or uncountable nouns.
error_reason: Teachers is plural, so do not use an with it.
keywords: a an, singular countable nouns

title: The for specific nouns
rule: Use the when both speaker and listener know which person or thing is meant.
explanation: The points to a specific noun.
correct_example_1: The book on the table is mine.
error_reason: A specific window needs the.
keywords: the, definite article, specific noun

title: Present continuous for now
rule: Use am/is/are + verb-ing for actions happening now or around now.
explanation: It describes temporary actions and current situations.
correct_example_1: She is reading at the moment.
correct_example_2: They are staying with friends this week.
corrected_example: She is reading at the moment.
error_reason: An action happening now usually needs the present continuous.
keywords: present continuous, now, am is are ing

title: Present simple or present continuous
rule: Use the present simple for routines and the present continuous for temporary actions.
explanation: Choose the tense by meaning.
correct_example_1: I work every day. / I am working today.
correct_example_2: She usually walks to school. / She is walking now.
error_reason: A regular routine usually takes the present simple.
keywords: present simple, present continuous, routines, temporary

title: Past simple regular verbs
rule: Add -ed to regular verbs in the past simple.
explanation: Use the past simple for finished actions in the past.
correct_example_1: We watched a film last night.
incorrect_example: We watch a film last night.
corrected_example: We watched a film last night.
error_reason: A finished past time needs the past simple form.
keywords: past simple, regular verbs, -ed

title: Irregular past simple verbs
rule: Some common verbs have irregular past forms and do not add -ed.
explanation: Learn the past forms of common irregular verbs.
error_reason: Go has an irregular past form: went.
keywords: irregular verbs, went, had, past simple

title: Past simple negatives and questions
rule: Use did not and did with the base verb in past simple negatives and questions.
explanation: After did, use the base form of the verb.
error_reason: After did, use the base verb arrive.
keywords: did not, did, past simple questions

title: Be going to for plans
rule: Use be going to for planned future actions and for strong predictions based on evidence.
explanation: It often refers to intention or clear signs.
correct_example_1: We are going to visit my parents tomorrow.
correct_example_2: Look at those clouds. It is going to rain.
incorrect_example: We go to visit my parents tomorrow.
corrected_example: We are going to visit my parents tomorrow.
error_reason: Future plans usually need be going to or another future form.
keywords: going to, future plans, predictions

title: Will for decisions and predictions
rule: Use will for spontaneous decisions, offers, and predictions.
explanation: Will is often used at the moment of speaking.
correct_example_1: I will help you with that.
correct_example_2: I think it will be busy today.
incorrect_example: I am helping you with that tomorrow.
corrected_example: I will help you with that.
error_reason: A spontaneous offer or decision often uses will.
keywords: will, future predictions, offers, decisions

title: Comparatives with short adjectives
rule: Use -er for many short adjectives, or more with longer adjectives.
explanation: Comparatives compare two people, places, or things.
correct_example_1: This bag is cheaper than that one.
correct_example_2: She is more careful than her brother.
incorrect_example: This bag is more cheap than that one.
corrected_example: This bag is cheaper than that one.
error_reason: Cheap is a short adjective, so use cheaper.
keywords: comparatives, -er, more than

title: Superlatives with adjectives
rule: Use -est for many short adjectives, or the most with longer adjectives.
explanation: Superlatives compare one thing with a group.
correct_example_1: It is the smallest room in the house.
correct_example_2: She is the most careful driver here.
incorrect_example: It is the more small room in the house.
corrected_example: It is the smallest room in the house.
error_reason: Small takes the superlative form smallest.
keywords: superlatives, -est, the most

title: Must for necessity
rule: Use must for strong necessity or obligation.
explanation: It shows something is necessary.
correct_example_1: You must wear a seat belt.
correct_example_2: I must call my mother tonight.
incorrect_example: You must to wear a seat belt.
corrected_example: You must wear a seat belt.
error_reason: Do not use to after must.
keywords: must, necessity, obligation

title: Have to for obligation
rule: Use have to for rules and outside obligations.
explanation: It often means the obligation comes from another person or rule.
correct_example_1: I have to start work at eight.
correct_example_2: She has to wear a uniform.
incorrect_example: I have start work at eight.
corrected_example: I have to start work at eight.
error_reason: Have to needs to before the verb.
keywords: have to, obligation, rules

title: Can for ability and permission
rule: Use can to talk about ability or to ask for and give permission.
explanation: Can does not change with the subject.
error_reason: Can does not take -s.
keywords: can, ability, permission

title: Must not and do not have to
rule: Must not means not allowed. Do not have to means not necessary.
explanation: These two forms have different meanings.
correct_example_2: You do not have to bring lunch.
incorrect_example: You mustn't bring lunch because it is not necessary.
corrected_example: You do not have to bring lunch.
error_reason: Must not means prohibition, not lack of necessity.
keywords: must not, do not have to, prohibition, necessity

title: Gerunds after like, love, and hate
rule: Use the -ing form after like, love, and hate when they mean enjoyment or preference.
explanation: These verbs are often followed by a gerund.
error_reason: After like, use the -ing form or a to-infinitive, not to reading.
keywords: gerund, -ing, like love hate

title: Infinitives after want and need
rule: Use the to-infinitive after want and need.
explanation: These verbs are followed by to + verb.
error_reason: Want is followed by a to-infinitive.
keywords: infinitive, to learn, want need

title: Present perfect for life experience
rule: Use have/has + past participle for experiences at an unspecified time.
explanation: The exact time is not important.
error_reason: Life experience often uses the present perfect when time is not specific.
keywords: present perfect, experience, have has past participle

title: Yet, already, and just
rule: Use yet in negative sentences and questions, already in positives, and just for very recent actions.
explanation: These words often go with the present perfect.
error_reason: Yet is usually used in negatives or questions, not positive statements.
keywords: yet already just, present perfect

title: Present perfect or past simple
rule: Use the present perfect for unfinished time or life experience, and the past simple for finished past time.
explanation: Time expressions help you choose the tense.
correct_example_1: I have seen that film. / I saw it yesterday.
correct_example_2: She has lived here for years. / She moved here in 2020.
incorrect_example: I have seen that film yesterday.
error_reason: Yesterday is finished past time, so use the past simple.
keywords: present perfect, past simple, finished time, unfinished time

title: Future plans with going to and present continuous
rule: Use be going to or the present continuous for future arrangements and plans.
explanation: Both forms can talk about future intentions or fixed arrangements.
correct_example_2: We are going to buy a new sofa.
error_reason: A future arrangement usually needs a future form.
keywords: future arrangements, present continuous, going to

title: First and second conditional basics
rule: Use the first conditional for possible future results and the second conditional for unreal or unlikely situations.
explanation: Choose the form by how possible the situation is.
correct_example_1: If it rains, we will stay at home.
correct_example_2: If I had more time, I would travel.
incorrect_example: If it will rain, we stay at home.
corrected_example: If it rains, we will stay at home.
error_reason: In first conditional if-clauses, use the present simple, not will.
keywords: first conditional, second conditional, if clauses

title: Zero conditional for facts
rule: Use the present simple in both clauses for general truths and facts.
explanation: This form describes something that is always true.
correct_example_1: If you heat water, it boils.
correct_example_2: If people do not sleep, they feel tired.
incorrect_example: If you heat water, it will boil.
corrected_example: If you heat water, it boils.
error_reason: General truths usually use the present simple in both clauses.
keywords: zero conditional, facts, general truths

title: Present simple passive
rule: Use am/is/are + past participle for the present simple passive.
explanation: The focus is on the action or the result, not the person who does it.
correct_example_2: These shoes are made in Italy.
error_reason: The passive needs be + past participle.
keywords: passive voice, present simple passive, is spoken

title: Past simple passive
rule: Use was/were + past participle for the past simple passive.
explanation: It talks about a finished action when the doer is not important.
correct_example_2: The letters were sent last week.
error_reason: The passive needs was or were plus a past participle.
keywords: passive voice, past simple passive, was repaired

title: Prepositions of time
rule: Use at for exact times, on for days and dates, and in for months, years, and longer periods.
explanation: Time prepositions depend on the type of time expression.
error_reason: Use on with days of the week.
keywords: at on in, prepositions of time

title: Prepositions of place
rule: Use in for enclosed spaces, on for surfaces, and at for points or places.
explanation: Choose the preposition by position.
correct_example_1: The keys are on the table.
incorrect_example: The keys are in the table.
corrected_example: The keys are on the table.
error_reason: A table is a surface, so use on.
keywords: prepositions of place, in on at

title: Present perfect continuous for duration
rule: Use have/has been + verb-ing to show an action that started in the past and continues now or has recently stopped.
explanation: It focuses on the length of time or recent activity.
correct_example_1: I have been waiting for an hour.
correct_example_2: She has been studying all morning.
incorrect_example: I am waiting for an hour.
corrected_example: I have been waiting for an hour.
error_reason: For an action lasting up to now, use the present perfect continuous.
keywords: present perfect continuous, duration, have been ing

topic: present perfect continuous versus present perfect
title: Present perfect simple or continuous
rule: Use the present perfect simple for completed results and the present perfect continuous for duration or recent activity.
explanation: Choose the form depending on what you want to emphasise.
correct_example_1: I have finished my work. / I have been working all day.
correct_example_2: She has written three emails. / She has been writing emails since lunch.
incorrect_example: I have been finishing my work.
error_reason: A completed result usually needs the present perfect simple.
keywords: present perfect simple, present perfect continuous, result duration

title: Past simple or present perfect in conversation
rule: Use the past simple for finished time and the present perfect for life experience or unfinished time.
explanation: Words like yesterday and last year usually take the past simple.
correct_example_1: I have been to Madrid. / I went there in 2022.
correct_example_2: She has just arrived. / She arrived five minutes ago.
error_reason: Yesterday is finished time, so use the past simple.
keywords: past simple, present perfect, finished time, experience

title: Future arrangements and intentions
rule: Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements and going to for intentions or plans.
explanation: Both can refer to the future, but they are used in slightly different ways.
correct_example_1: We are meeting the client on Friday.
correct_example_2: I am going to start a new course in September.
incorrect_example: We meet the client on Friday.
corrected_example: We are meeting the client on Friday.
error_reason: A fixed future arrangement needs a future form.
keywords: future forms, present continuous, going to, arrangements

title: Will or going to
rule: Use will for immediate decisions and predictions, and going to for plans or evidence-based predictions.
explanation: The choice depends on the reason for the future form.
correct_example_1: I think it will rain later.
correct_example_2: Look at the sky. It is going to rain.
incorrect_example: I am going to help you now.
error_reason: An immediate decision usually uses will.
keywords: will, going to, predictions, immediate decisions

title: Must, may, and might for deduction
rule: Use must for a strong deduction, may or might for a possible deduction, and cannot for something that is impossible.
explanation: These modals show how certain you are.
correct_example_1: He must be at work; his car is outside.
incorrect_example: He must to be at work.
error_reason: Do not use to after modal verbs.
keywords: must may might cannot, deduction

title: Should and ought to for advice
rule: Use should or ought to to give advice or say what is right.
explanation: These modals are common in polite advice.
incorrect_example: You should to see a doctor.
error_reason: Should is followed by the base verb.
keywords: should, ought to, advice

title: Could and was able to
rule: Use could for general past ability and was able to for a specific successful action in the past.
explanation: Could is not usually used for one finished success.
correct_example_1: When I was young, I could run fast.
correct_example_2: She was able to open the window.
incorrect_example: She could open the window after trying for an hour.
corrected_example: She was able to open the window after trying for an hour.
error_reason: A specific past success usually uses was able to.
keywords: could, was able to, past ability

title: Remember, forget, and stop
rule: Remember and forget can be followed by a gerund or infinitive with different meanings. Stop usually changes meaning too.
explanation: The verb form changes the meaning.
correct_example_1: I remember locking the door. / Please remember to lock the door.
correct_example_2: He stopped smoking. / He stopped to smoke.
incorrect_example: I remember to lock the door yesterday.
corrected_example: I remembered to lock the door yesterday.
error_reason: For a past event, remembered is needed, not remember.
keywords: remember forget stop, gerund infinitive, meaning

title: Gerunds after prepositions
rule: Use the -ing form after a preposition.
explanation: After in, for, at, about, and similar words, use a gerund.
correct_example_1: She is interested in learning French.
incorrect_example: She is interested in learn French.
corrected_example: She is interested in learning French.
error_reason: After a preposition, use the -ing form.
keywords: gerund after preposition, interested in, without saying

title: Infinitive after adjectives
rule: Use a to-infinitive after many adjectives.
explanation: Common patterns include happy to, easy to, and difficult to.
error_reason: After many adjectives, use to + verb.
keywords: to-infinitive, adjectives, easy to

title: Passive with modal verbs
rule: Use modal verb + be + past participle in the passive.
explanation: This form is common in rules and formal writing.
correct_example_1: The report must be finished today.
corrected_example: The report must be finished today.
error_reason: The passive after a modal needs be plus a past participle.
keywords: passive voice, modal verbs, must be finished

title: Passive with present perfect
rule: Use have/has been + past participle in the passive present perfect.
explanation: It describes a result up to now.
error_reason: The passive perfect form needs been.
keywords: passive voice, present perfect passive, has been cleaned

title: First conditional with unless and when
rule: Use unless to mean if not, and when for a future situation that is expected.
explanation: These words are common in real future conditions.
correct_example_1: Unless it rains, we will go out.
correct_example_2: When I finish work, I will call you.
incorrect_example: Unless it will rain, we will go out.
corrected_example: Unless it rains, we will go out.
error_reason: In the unless-clause, use the present simple.
keywords: unless, when, first conditional

title: Second conditional for imaginary situations
rule: Use if + past simple and would + base verb for imaginary or unlikely present or future situations.
explanation: It describes a situation that is not real or not likely.
correct_example_1: If I had a car, I would drive to work.
correct_example_2: If she lived closer, she would visit more often.
incorrect_example: If I would have a car, I would drive to work.
corrected_example: If I had a car, I would drive to work.
error_reason: In second conditional if-clauses, use the past simple, not would have.
keywords: second conditional, would, imaginary situations

title: Third conditional for past regret
rule: Use if + past perfect and would have + past participle to talk about unreal past situations.
explanation: It is often used for regrets or different past results.
correct_example_1: If I had studied, I would have passed.
correct_example_2: If they had left earlier, they would have caught the train.
incorrect_example: If I studied, I would have passed.
corrected_example: If I had studied, I would have passed.
error_reason: Third conditional needs the past perfect in the if-clause.
keywords: third conditional, past regret, would have

title: Relative pronouns
rule: Use who for people, which for things, and that for people or things in defining clauses.
explanation: Relative pronouns connect two sentences.
correct_example_1: The woman who called is my aunt.
correct_example_2: The phone that I bought is new.
incorrect_example: The woman which called is my aunt.
corrected_example: The woman who called is my aunt.
error_reason: Who is used for people, not which.
keywords: relative pronouns, who which that

title: Reported speech changes
rule: In reported speech, present simple often changes to past simple.
explanation: Tenses usually move back when reporting what someone said.
correct_example_1: He said that he was tired.
correct_example_2: She told me that she liked the film.
incorrect_example: He said that he is tired.
corrected_example: He said that he was tired.
error_reason: In reported speech, the tense often changes back.
keywords: reported speech, tense backshift, said that

title: No article for general plural and uncountable nouns
rule: Do not use an article when talking generally about plural nouns or uncountable nouns.
explanation: Use no article for general meaning.
error_reason: This is a general statement, so no article is needed.
keywords: articles, no article, general nouns

title: Quantifiers with countable and uncountable nouns
rule: Use many and few with countable nouns, and much and little with uncountable nouns.
explanation: Match the quantifier to the noun type.
error_reason: Homework is uncountable, so use much.
keywords: many much few little, countable uncountable
